title: Communication and Advertising
description: Ten standalone texts about slogans, billboards, packaging, persuasion and the old machines that carried messages.

lessons.title: How a Slogan Is Born
lessons.summary: Two writers at an agency spend an afternoon finding a slogan for a family company's frozen waffles.
lessons.text:
The client was a family company called Hartwell, and the product was a frozen waffle. Hartwell had made waffles in the same small factory for forty years, and the founder's granddaughter wanted a slogan that would carry the brand into supermarkets across the country. The task went to Nora Quinn, a senior writer at a modest agency, and to Sam, a young writer who had joined the team that spring.

They began, as Nora always began, by eating the product. She toasted four waffles and set them on a plate between their notebooks. Sam devoured his first waffle in under a minute. Nora watched him devour it and wrote a single word at the top of a clean page: hunger.

The first hour produced nothing worth keeping. Sam's early ideas were cheesy, and he knew it. He offered rhymes about golden mornings and smiling suns, each one more cheesy than the last, until he laughed and admitted that he would never buy a waffle from a sun with a face. Nora told him that cheesy ideas were not a failure. They were the noise a mind makes before it finds the signal.

By the second hour, Sam had grown restless. He tapped his pen against the table and asked whether they might postpone the work until the morning. Nora refused to postpone it. She had learned that a restless mind is often close to something.

Instead, she asked him to describe exactly how he used to eat waffles as a boy. "We didn't really eat them," he said. "We hoovered them up. My brother and I could hoover up a whole box before the school bus came." Nora asked what they had talked about during those hurried breakfasts.

"Tomorrow, mostly," Sam said. "Tomorrow's test, tomorrow's game, whatever was coming next."

"Ohh," said Nora, drawing the sound out slowly, and Sam recognized the long "ohh" she made whenever an idea had just walked into the room.

The rest of the afternoon was a matter of sharpening. A slogan, she explained, is rarely invented in a single flash. It is sharpened, like a pencil, by cutting away everything that does not belong. They wrote forty versions of the same thought, and some were sloppy, with too many words or a rhythm that limped. Nora crossed out the sloppy ones at once, and soon Sam was crossing out his own. Each version was shorter than the one before, and each one sharpened the picture of a family at a kitchen table, talking about the day ahead.

The line they sent to Hartwell the next morning was five words long: "Breakfast for tomorrow's big plans." The granddaughter called that afternoon to say yes.

Questions:
What did Nora and Sam do before they started writing?
They ate the product, and Sam devoured his first waffle in under a minute.
Why did Nora refuse to postpone the work?
She had learned that a restless mind is often close to something good.
What did Sam and his brother talk about at breakfast?
They talked about tomorrow: tomorrow's test, tomorrow's game, and whatever was coming next.
How, according to Nora, is a slogan made?
It is sharpened like a pencil, by cutting away everything that does not belong.

lessons.title: The Long Life of the Billboard
lessons.summary: A short history of the billboard, from canal boats and farm fields to wartime posters and modern screens.
lessons.text:
Long before anyone spoke of advertising campaigns, merchants painted their names on walls. The billboard as we know it, however, is a child of the nineteenth century, when printers learned to produce large posters at low cost. In the busiest streets, posters were pasted over posters until the paper grew as thick as a book.

The billboard truly flourished when people began to travel. Along rivers and canals, sign painters raised enormous boards where passengers on slow boats would see them for minutes at a time. A waterway made an ideal audience: the traveler could not change the route, and there was little else to look at. When the automobile arrived, the same logic moved from the waterway to the highway. Farmers discovered that a corner of a field facing the road was worth more to an advertiser than to a cow. In Europe, where land is measured in hectares, a farmer might rent out a strip smaller than a tenth of a hectare and earn a steady income from it for years.

The fortunes of the billboard have always followed the fortunes of the economy. In prosperous years, the boards multiplied along every road out of town, each one promising a better car or a cleaner kitchen. When the prosperous years ended, many stood empty, their faded paper hanging in strips.

Weather was the old enemy. On windy days the paper tore at the edges, and a single thunderstorm could ruin a month of advertising in an afternoon. After a thunderstorm, crews in trucks drove from board to board with buckets of paste, and posters were replaced periodically even in calm weather, because sun and dust slowly drained the color out of them. The wooden boards themselves had to be painted again periodically.

In wartime, the billboard changed its voice. Instead of selling soap, it asked citizens to save metal, grow vegetables and buy government bonds. These wartime posters appealed to patriotism, and their patriotism was simple and direct: a flag, a determined face, a few words.

After the war, designers influenced by modern art brought geometric shapes to the highway: bold circles, triangles and stripes that a driver could grasp at a glance. A driver passing at sixty miles an hour has perhaps five seconds to read a sign, so designers learned to cut their messages to a handful of words. A board with nineteen words on it, one old designer liked to say, is not a billboard but a letter, and nobody reads nineteen words at sixty miles an hour.

Today many billboards are screens that change their message every few seconds. The paste buckets have gone, but the old rule remains: say one thing, say it large, and say it quickly.

Questions:
How did a farmer earn money from a billboard?
He rented out a small strip of land facing the road, sometimes smaller than a tenth of a hectare.
What did weather do to billboards?
Windy days tore the paper, and a single thunderstorm could ruin a month of advertising.
What did wartime posters ask citizens to do?
They asked citizens to save metal, grow vegetables and buy government bonds.
What did designers bring to the highway after the war?
They brought geometric shapes, such as bold circles, triangles and stripes.
Why is a board with nineteen words a bad idea?
A driver has only a few seconds to read a sign, and nobody reads nineteen words at sixty miles an hour.

lessons.title: The Color of the Bottle
lessons.summary: A small juice company redesigns its bottle and learns what research says about color and taste.
lessons.text:
When the small juice company Fernhill decided to redesign its bottles, its two owners, Clara and Owen, began with a question that sounds simple: what color should a drink be? To answer it, they hired Helen Ashby, a consultant who had spent ten years reading the scholarly literature pertaining to color and taste. She began by correcting a common belief.

"No color is inherently calm or inherently exciting," she told them. "We learn what colors mean, mostly from the products we have already bought." The scholarly research, she explained, shows that the strongest effect comes not from any single color but from the compatibility between a color and what we expect to find inside. A lemon drink in a brown bottle feels wrong before anyone tastes it. When the compatibility is poor, people often say the drink tastes strange, even when the recipe is the same.

Helen then showed them a study pertaining to sweetness. Volunteers tasted the same drink dyed in several shades of red, and the deeper red samples seemed sweeter to them. The effect, however, was not proportional. Doubling the amount of red did not make the drink seem twice as sweet; after a certain point, it simply looked artificial. The relation between color and taste, she said, is real but rarely proportional.

This mattered to Fernhill, because the company had promised its customers a drink without any artificial additive. Its new berry juice was a deep purple, and the purple came from red cabbage. Clara admitted that the word "cabbage" did not sound delicious, but Helen pointed out that cabbage juice has been used to color food for a very long time, and that many shoppers now read the label precisely to make sure there is no additive they cannot pronounce.

The shape of the bottle came next. Helen brought two versions, one round and one slender. In her tests, people described the slender bottle as more elegant, though they also guessed that it held less juice, which was not true. Owen liked the slender one at once.

The label was the last problem. The first design used six inks, which looked rich but was far from economical. Helen suggested two colors, purple and a warm white, which was more economical to print and easier to read on a crowded shelf. She also warned them about an imbalance in the early drawings: the bright label was so loud that the dark juice behind it seemed dull. Correcting the imbalance meant making the label smaller, so that the color of the drink itself could speak.

Six months later, Fernhill's purple bottle stood on the shelves of forty stores, with a small white label and nothing inside but fruit and cabbage.

Questions:
What did Helen say about the meaning of colors?
She said that no color is inherently calm or exciting, and that we learn what colors mean.
What does the research show about compatibility?
It shows that the strongest effect comes from the compatibility between a color and what we expect inside.
Why was the effect of red on sweetness not proportional?
Doubling the red did not make the drink seem twice as sweet, and after a certain point it looked artificial.
Where did the purple color of the berry juice come from?
It came from red cabbage, because Fernhill had promised a drink without any artificial additive.

lessons.title: A Writer of Small Sentences
lessons.summary: A magazine profile of Ruth Calloway, a prolific advertising writer who still works in a loft at seventy.
lessons.text:
Ruth Calloway works in a loft above a bakery, and the smell of bread rises through the floor all morning. The loft has one long table and a wall covered with index cards, each holding a single sentence. At seventy, she is one of the most prolific writers in the business. By her own count, she has written more than twelve thousand headlines, and she still comes to the loft five days a week.

She did not plan this life. In her twenties she was a wanderer, moving from city to city with one suitcase and no particular ambition. For a wanderer, a hotel bar was a natural place to stop, and for three years she worked as a bartender in Chicago. She says the bar taught her more about writing than any classroom. A good bartender listens. Behind the counter, she heard how people actually talk: how they ask for what they want, and how they hesitate. She kept a notebook under the counter and filled it with the phrases she heard.

Her first job in an agency was a baptism of fire. On her second day, the senior writer fell ill, and Ruth was asked to produce a radio campaign for a furniture store by Friday. She wrote all night, three nights in a row. The campaign was not brilliant, she admits, but it was finished on time, and after that baptism no deadline ever frightened her.

She once dreamed of something grander. In her forties she wrote a screenplay about two sisters who run a lighthouse. The screenplay was praised by two producers and bought by neither, and she keeps it in a drawer without regret. "I learned that I am a writer of small sentences," she says. "Some people build cathedrals. I make good doors."

It would be easy for someone with her experience to become cynical about advertising, and she has met plenty of cynical colleagues. She is not one of them. She believes that a clear, honest sentence can help a person make a decision, and that is enough for her. When younger writers bring her their work, she reads it with real humility, as if she might learn something. Often, she says, she does.

That humility explains much of the admiration she receives. At industry dinners, younger writers line up to speak with her, and she is gracious with every one of them, remembering names and asking about their projects. She is just as open in her admiration for good work, even when it comes from a rival agency.

On Thursday evenings, the loft changes its purpose. Ruth pushes the long table against the wall and dances the tango with a group of friends. She took up the tango at sixty. "It is like writing," she says. "Every step must be necessary."

Questions:
How prolific is Ruth Calloway?
She is very prolific: she has written more than twelve thousand headlines.
What did Ruth learn as a bartender?
She learned how people actually talk, and she filled a notebook with the phrases she heard.
Why was her first job a baptism of fire?
On her second day she had to produce a radio campaign by Friday, so she wrote all night for three nights.
What happened to her screenplay?
Two producers praised the screenplay, but neither bought it, and she keeps it in a drawer.
How does Ruth treat younger writers?
She reads their work with humility and is gracious with every one of them.

lessons.title: Why We Trust a Stranger's Word
lessons.summary: An essay on why testimonials persuade us, and how evidence differs from a good story.
lessons.text:
Few forms of advertising are as quietly effective as the testimonial, in which an ordinary person tells us that a product worked. We may doubt a company that praises itself, but we listen when a stranger who looks like us says the same thing. Psychologists explain this readiness to believe in simple terms. For most of human history, the experience of the people around us was the best information we had, and our readiness to follow it saved us a great deal of trouble.

The trouble begins when the stranger is not quite what he seems. Consider an invented but typical case. A company called Vantor sells a supplement that claims to raise testosterone, a hormone that helps the body build muscle. Its website shows a dozen smiling men who say they feel younger and stronger. None of them mentions the dosage, and the label recommends a dosage far higher than anything tested in a laboratory. The stories sound sincere, but they tell us nothing about whether the pills affect testosterone at all.

A second case is a skin cream we will call Clearbrook. Its advertisements feature a woman who says the cream healed a lesion on her cheek in a week. A lesion, in medical language, is any area of damaged skin or tissue, and many a small lesion heals on its own in a week, cream or no cream. Her story may be true and still prove nothing.

Real evidence looks different. In a supervised trial, one group of volunteers receives the product and another receives an identical copy of it with nothing active inside, and neither the volunteers nor the doctors who supervise them know who received which. Such studies are slow, and the important details often sit in an appendix at the end of the report: the dosage, the number of volunteers, the people who dropped out. A careful reader learns to turn to the appendix first.

When testimonials are invented, the law can be strict. In a lawsuit that I followed as a reporter some years ago, a marketing manager gave a deposition, a statement made under oath before the trial, in which she admitted that several "customers" in her company's advertisements were paid actors. Her deposition ended the case within a month.

None of this means that testimonials are worthless. A friend's honest report about a restaurant is useful, and online reviews have empowered consumers who once had only the seller's word. The danger is that a lively story can perpetuate a weak claim for years, simply because stories are easier to remember than numbers. An empowered consumer enjoys the story but still asks for the evidence, and refuses to let a charming face perpetuate a myth.

Questions:
Why are we ready to believe a stranger who praises a product?
For most of human history, the experience of the people around us was the best information we had.
What is missing from the stories on Vantor's website?
None of the men mentions the dosage, and the stories say nothing about whether the pills affect testosterone.
Why does the woman's story about the lesion prove nothing?
Many small lesions heal on their own in a week, with or without cream.
What happens in a supervised trial?
One group receives the product and another receives a copy with nothing active inside, and nobody knows who received which.
What did the marketing manager admit in her deposition?
She admitted that several customers in the advertisements were paid actors.

lessons.title: The Ethics of Persuasion, Weighed Calmly
lessons.summary: An opinion column that sets the case against advertising beside the case for it.
lessons.text:
Advertising has always had its critics, and some of them describe it in almost sinister terms: a hidden machine that reaches into our minds and moves our hands toward our wallets. Its defenders reply that there is nothing sinister about telling people what is for sale. Both sides have a point, and the question becomes clearer if we take their arguments one at a time.

The critics' strongest argument concerns people in difficulty. A loan company that covers the poorest part of a city with posters is aiming at needy families at the moment when they are least able to compare offers, and the needy are rarely the ones who read the small print. Critics also point to the societal effects of advertising as a whole. The steady message that happiness can be bought, repeated thousands of times a year, may shape a society's values in ways that no single advertisement intends. Such societal effects are hard to measure, but that does not make them imaginary.

History offers further examples. Old advertisements for household products sometimes played on marital fears, suggesting that a wife whose kitchen floor was not perfectly clean might lose her husband's affection. Few people today would defend marital anxiety as a selling point. Other advertisements promised social superiority: buy this car, and the whole street will envy you. Claims of superiority over a rival product are now regulated in many countries, and a company that calls its soap "the best" may be asked to prove it.

The defenders' argument is equally serious. Advertising pays for much of the journalism we read, and a well-run newspaper keeps a strict segregation between its reporters and its advertising department. That segregation, when it is respected, allows a paper to criticize the very companies that buy its pages. Advertising also helps newcomers. An insurgent brand, a small company challenging a giant, has few other ways to reach customers who have bought the same product for decades. Without advertising, the insurgent might never be heard, and the giant would face no competition.

Defenders also note that advertising has helped to break taboos. Subjects that were once taboo, such as mental health, entered public conversation partly through campaigns that were courageous enough to name them. A courageous campaign can make a difficult subject ordinary, and that is a public good.

Where does this leave us? Perhaps persuasion is a tool, neither good nor evil in itself. We do not want every poster to list a product's faults brutally, and a brutally honest advertisement would probably sell nothing. But we can reasonably ask that persuasion be honest, that it not take advantage of people in trouble, and that it be clearly labeled as what it is.

Questions:
Why do critics object to loan posters in the poorest part of a city?
The posters aim at needy families when they are least able to compare offers.
What did some old advertisements suggest about marital life?
They suggested that a wife whose kitchen floor was not perfectly clean might lose her husband's affection.
Why does a newspaper keep a segregation between reporters and advertising?
It allows the paper to criticize the very companies that buy its pages.
How does advertising help an insurgent brand?
It gives a small company a way to reach customers who have bought a giant's product for decades.
What can a courageous campaign do?
It can make a difficult subject ordinary.

lessons.title: The Semaphore and the Telegraph
lessons.summary: How messages learned to travel faster than a horse, first by wooden arms on towers and then by wire.
lessons.text:
For most of history, a message could travel no faster than the person who carried it. When a king wished to speak with a foreign ruler, he sent an envoy, and the envoy rode or sailed for weeks. By the time an envoy arrived, the situation he had been sent to discuss had often changed completely.

The first serious attempt to beat the horse came from France in 1794. Claude Chappe and his brothers built a chain of towers on hills between Paris and Lille, each within sight of the next. On top of each tower stood a tall post with wooden arms that could turn. An operator set the arms in a certain position, which stood for a letter or a phrase, and the operator in the next tower, watching through a telescope, copied it. This optical telegraph, often called the semaphore, could carry a short message about 140 miles in less than an hour. It was useless at night and in fog, however, and when a new building blocked the view, a tower had to be moved. Each relocation interrupted the whole line, and a single relocation could take weeks.

The electric telegraph, which spread in the middle of the nineteenth century, worked by day or night, in fog or rain. A message traveled along a wire as a series of short and long pulses. Every telegraph office kept a ledger in which a clerk recorded each message: the time it arrived, the number of words and the price. Because customers paid by the word, a whole society learned to write with remarkable economy, and some historians see the telegram as an ancestor of the modern slogan.

Merchants saw its value at once. An exporter who learned the price of cotton abroad a day before his competitors could make a fortune, and exporters soon became some of the telegraph's best customers. Scientists found uses too. An astronomer could send a signal at a precise moment, and an astronomer hundreds of miles away could note it on his own clock, which allowed them to fix the position of places on the map with new accuracy.

Laying a cable across the floor of the Atlantic was a titanic task. The first cable worked for only a few weeks, and success came in 1866, after years of titanic effort. Other cables reached remote islands. For an islander who had waited weeks for a mail ship, the change was enormous: islanders could now learn of events in a distant capital on the same day.

In 1868, when the House of Representatives voted for the impeachment of President Andrew Johnson, the story reached newspapers across the country within hours, and the impeachment became an event the nation followed almost as it happened.

Telegraph operators sometimes showed great bravery, staying at their keys during floods and fires to warn the next town. Their bravery is rarely remembered, but it saved many lives.

Questions:
How did the semaphore work?
An operator set wooden arms on a tower in a certain position, and the operator in the next tower copied it.
What did a clerk record in the ledger?
The clerk recorded the time each message arrived, the number of words and the price.
Why did exporters like the telegraph?
Merchants saw its value at once. An exporter who learned prices abroad before his competitors could make a fortune.
What did the cables mean for islanders?
Islanders could learn of events in a distant capital on the same day.

lessons.title: The Sparrow and the Pipes
lessons.summary: A city engineer uses a cartoon sparrow to persuade residents to stop pouring fat and solvents down the drain.
lessons.text:
In the city of Larkfield, the problem was invisible until it was enormous. For years, residents had poured cooking fat down their kitchen sinks without a second thought. Warm fat runs like water, but in the cold pipes under the streets it hardens, sticks to the walls and slowly narrows them. One January night, a main pipe under Mill Street could take no more. The rupture flooded three basements and closed the street for a week, and the local newspaper described the event as a meltdown of the city's plumbing. The word meltdown appeared in the headline, and it stayed in people's minds.

The engineer in charge of the repairs, Dana Ruiz, knew that new pipes would not solve the problem. The plumbing was not the real cause; habits were. Inspections showed that the fat was not alone. Many residents also poured paint solvent and other cleaning chemicals down the drain, and the solvent damaged the pipes from the inside. Dana proposed a public campaign to change both habits.

Her first obstacle was bureaucracy. The campaign needed approval from three departments, each with its own forms, and for four months the plan moved slowly from desk to desk. Dana did not argue with the bureaucracy. Instead, she filled in every form on the day it arrived and attached a photograph of the flooded basements to each one. The approval came in the spring.

The campaign itself was gentle. Dana and a local designer created a cartoon sparrow named Pip, a small brown bird with a worried face and a tiny wrench. They chose a sparrow because sparrows live on every street in the city, just as the pipes run under every street. Pip appeared on posters, on the sides of buses and on stickers that children could put on the kitchen sink. His message was always the same: let the fat cool, pour it into a can, and put the can in the trash.

For paint solvent and chemicals, the city needed a better answer than a poster. Larkfield had once held a free collection day for household chemicals, but the program had been canceled years earlier to save money. Dana persuaded the city council to reinstate it. The council agreed to reinstate the collection day four times a year, and on the first one, residents brought more than two thousand containers.

The habit changed slowly but steadily. Teachers used the little sparrow in science lessons, and children began to correct their parents at the sink. Within two years, the number of blocked pipes in the city had fallen by half. Nobody in Larkfield now remembers the exact words on the posters, but almost everyone remembers the worried little bird.

Questions:
What caused the rupture under Mill Street?
Cooking fat had hardened in the cold pipes and slowly narrowed them.
Why did Dana believe that new pipes would not solve the problem?
She believed that the plumbing was not the real cause; the residents' habits were.
How did Dana deal with the bureaucracy?
She filled in every form on the day it arrived and attached a photograph of the flooded basements.
Why did the designers choose a sparrow?
Sparrows live on every street in the city, just as the pipes run under every street.
What did the city council agree to reinstate?
It agreed to reinstate the free collection day for household chemicals four times a year.

lessons.title: A Poster for the Barbarians
lessons.summary: A small Swiss museum needs a poster for its new exhibition, and an unusual image brings the visitors in.
lessons.text:
The museum stands on the main square of a small town in one of the mountain cantons of Switzerland. It occupies a single old house, and it survives on a modest endowment left by a local family a century ago. The endowment pays for heating and for two salaries, but not for advertising, so when the director, Lena Brunner, planned a new exhibition, she knew that one poster would have to do the work of an entire campaign.

The exhibition was the idea of Marco Steiner, the museum's archaeologist. For twenty years he had studied the people who lived in the valley before the Romans arrived. The Romans called them barbarians, a word that originally meant little more than "people who do not speak our language." Marco wanted to show that these so-called barbarians were skilled farmers, workers in metal and traders. He called the exhibition "Who Were the Barbarians?"

His favorite object was a bronze ornament shaped like a horse. It had an unusual history. A retired teacher had bought it for a few francs at a flea market in the next canton, thinking it was a cheap modern copy. Years later, she showed it to the archaeologist, who recognized it at once as genuine and more than two thousand years old. The flea market ornament became the heart of the exhibition.

Lena gave the poster to a young designer from the town. She expected a photograph of the ornament, but the designer proposed something surreal: a Roman soldier's helmet, filled with wild flowers, resting in a green meadow, with the bronze horse standing on top of it. The image was strange, but it was not confusing. It suggested, in a calm and surreal way, that the Roman world had passed and the valley had remained.

Lena hesitated for a day and then agreed. The posters went up in train stations across the region, and the response was warmer than anyone in the little museum had expected. The town went gaga over the image. Shops asked for copies to hang in their windows, and a local bakery made cookies in the shape of the horse. Even people who were not interested in archaeology went a little gaga over the helmet full of flowers.

The most important result, however, came from the schools. Teachers in the canton began to plan an excursion to the museum, and by the autumn more than forty classes had booked a visit. On each excursion, Marco told the children the story of the ornament from the flea market, and at the end he asked them a simple question: who were the barbarians? Most of the children answered that they were people very much like us.

Questions:
How does the museum pay for heating and salaries?
It survives on a modest endowment left by a local family a century ago.
What did the word "barbarians" originally mean?
It meant little more than people who do not speak our language.
Where did the bronze ornament come from?
A retired teacher bought it at a flea market, and the archaeologist recognized it as genuine.
What did the surreal poster show?
It showed a Roman helmet filled with wild flowers, with the bronze horse standing on top of it.
What did the teachers in the canton do?
They planned an excursion to the museum, and more than forty classes booked a visit.

lessons.title: One Minute of Rockets
lessons.summary: A science teacher makes a short video to attract new members to his school's rocket club.
lessons.text:
Every September, the clubs at Brookside Middle School compete for new members, and every September the rocket club loses. The chess club has trophies, the drama club has costumes, and the rocket club, as its leader Tom Avery admits, has six loyal students and a box of cardboard tubes. This year Tom decided to advertise. The school allowed each club to show a one-minute video at the first assembly, and Tom resolved that his minute would be the best one.

He began with equipment. The club's old launcher was a wooden frame with a cracked base, and it looked as tired as it was. Tom went on a modest shopping spree at the hardware store: plywood, screws, a can of red paint and a long, thick elastic cord. It was the only shopping spree of his teaching career, and he kept the receipt on his desk as a reminder. Over two weekends, he and the students built a new launcher. The elastic cord was stretched between two posts, and a foam rocket rested in the middle, held by a simple clip. When the clip was released, the elastic snapped forward and the rocket flew higher than the school roof.

Filming took a single windy afternoon on the football field. Tom wanted the video to show not only rockets but the feeling of launching them. He filmed the countdown from close up: the students' faces, the red launcher, and the hands of a girl named Maya, who held the clip so tightly that her knuckles turned white. Her white knuckles, Tom thought, said more about adrenaline than any explanation could. When the rocket flew, the students shouted, and the adrenaline of that moment was clear on every face.

The best shot came from patience rather than luck. Tom borrowed a phone that could record in slow motion, and on the ninth launch he caught the rocket rising against a deep blue sky, turning slowly, with a thin cloud behind it. On the screen it looked unreal, like a scene from a film about space. "That's unreal," said one of the boys, and Tom used his words as the last line of the video, followed by the time and place of the club's first meeting.

The video played at the assembly between the chess club and the drama club. The applause was polite but not overwhelming, and Tom went back to his classroom unsure of the result. Then the video became a sleeper success. A parent shared it online, other parents passed it on, and over the following weeks it was watched thousands of times. A sleeper, as people in film say, is a work that starts quietly and finds its audience slowly.

By October, the rocket club had thirty-one members, and Tom had to build a second launcher.

Questions:
What did Tom buy on his shopping spree?
He bought plywood, screws, a can of red paint and a long, thick elastic cord.
How did the new launcher work?
When the clip was released, the elastic cord snapped forward and sent the foam rocket into the air.
What did Maya's white knuckles show?
They showed the adrenaline and tension of the countdown.
Why did the boy say "That's unreal"?
In slow motion, the rocket rising against the blue sky looked like a scene from a film about space.
What is a sleeper success?
It is a work that starts quietly and finds its audience slowly.
